**Exercise 1.**

In R, work with the package fpp3 and load the data set books. The data set books contains the daily sales of paperback and hardcover books at the same store. The task is to forecast the next four days’ sales for paperback and hardcover books.

a. Plot the series and discuss the main features of the data.

```{r}
#rm(list = ls())

library(fpp2)

head(books)

autoplot(books) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Book Sales",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Number of Books Sold"
  )
```

b. Use simple exponential smoothing with the ses function (setting initial="simple") and explore different values of α for the paperback series. Record the within-sample SSE for the one-step forecasts. Plot SSE against αand find which value of αworks best. What is the effect of αon the forecasts?

Step 1: Test different values of α

```{r}
library(forecast)

alphas <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)

sse <- numeric(length(alphas))

for (i in seq_along(alphas)) {
  fit <- ses(books[, "Paperback"],
             alpha = alphas[i],
             initial = "simple",
             h = 4)

  sse[i] <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)
}

results <- data.frame(alpha = alphas, SSE = sse)

print(results)
```

Step 2: Plot SSE against α (lower is better for SSE)

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(results, aes(x = alpha, y = SSE)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "SSE vs Alpha",
    x = "Alpha",
    y = "Sum of Squared Errors"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

c. Now let ses select the optimal value of α. Use this value to generate forecasts for the next four days. Compare your results with 2.

```{r}
fit_opt <- ses(
  books[, "Paperback"],
  initial = "simple",
  h = 4
)

summary(fit_opt)

autoplot(fit_opt) +
  labs(
    title = "SES Forecast for Paperback Sales",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Paperback Sales"
  )
```

d. Repeat but with initial="optimal". How much difference does an optimal initial level make?

```{r}

fit_opt_initial <- ses(
  books[, "Paperback"],
  initial = "optimal",
  h = 4
)

summary(fit_opt_initial)

```

**Exercise 2.**

Use the data set books from the package fpp3, to repeat the analysis with several variants of a Holt’s model:

1. A Holt’s model with the holt function in R. Summarize the results, plot the series and add the past forecasts. Start first with some random choices for α and ˜β(etc.) and proceed after checking and choosing the model with the optimal choices for them.

Note: there are some constraints on the parameters: 0 < α < 1, 0 ⩽ ˜β ⩽ 1, 0 < γ < 1−α, 0.8 < Φ <0.98. 
Parameter γ is only needed for seasonality effect. Parameter Φ is needed in case of damping effect.

```{r}
library(forecast)

holt_manual <- holt(
  books[, "Paperback"],
  alpha = 0.2,
  beta = 0.1,
  h = 4
)

summary(holt_manual)

autoplot(holt_manual) +
  autolayer(fitted(holt_manual), series = "Fitted") +
  labs(
    title = "Holt's Linear Trend Method",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Paperback Sales"
  )
```
Optimize Holt's parameters

```{r}
holt_opt <- holt(
  books[, "Paperback"],
  h = 4
)

summary(holt_opt)
```
2. A Holt’s model with damped trend (see options in ?holt). Summarize it, plot the series and add the past forecasts.

```{r}

holt_damped <- holt(
  books[, "Paperback"],
  damped = TRUE,
  h = 4
)

summary(holt_damped)

autoplot(holt_damped) +
  autolayer(fitted(holt_damped), series = "Fitted") +
  labs(
    title = "Holt's Damped Trend Method",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Paperback Sales"
  )

```
3. A Holt’s model with the ets function. Summarize it, plot the decomposition, plot the forecast and add the past forecasts.

```{r}

library(forecast)

ets_fit <- ets(books[, "Paperback"])

summary(ets_fit)

autoplot(forecast(ets_fit, h = 4)) +
  autolayer(fitted(ets_fit), series = "Fitted") +
  labs(
    title = "ETS Forecast for Paperback Sales",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Paperback Sales"
  )

```
Inspecting the estimated components:

```{r}
autoplot(ets_fit)
```

Exercise 3. 

Use the domotic data set (Domotic2.xlsx) available in Moodle under datasets. It was retrieved from http://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/SML2010. You can use this link to see a description of the data set. In this exercise, the weather temperature is to be predicted (WeatherTemperature). This is indeed an important information to set the working parameters of the domotic house.

1. Load the data, take only the data of April (18.04.2012 - 30.04.2012) and the temperature column (Temperature_Comedor_Sensor) and plot them. Do you think it can be predicted using a Holt-Winters method? Why?

Step 1: Load the Excel file in R

```{r}
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

domotic <- read_excel(file.choose('/Users/helianferraris/Desktop/Forecasting with Applications in Business/Practical 8/Domotic2.xlsx'))

head(domotic)

```

Step 2: Select the April observations

```{r}

april <- domotic %>%
  mutate(
    datetime = as.POSIXct(
      paste(
        format(Date, "%Y-%m-%d"),
        format(Time, "%H:%M:%S")
      ),
      format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
      tz = "UTC"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    datetime >= as.POSIXct("2012-04-18", tz = "UTC"),
    datetime < as.POSIXct("2012-05-01", tz = "UTC")
  ) %>%
  arrange(datetime)

```

Step 3: Plot the temperature

```{r}

ggplot(april, aes(
  x = datetime,
  y = Temperature_Comedor_Sensor
)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Dining Room Temperature - April 2012",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(
    date_breaks = "2 days",
    date_labels = "%d %b"

```
2. Compute the hourly averages over this period and build a ts object with them (seasonality 24 hours). Use this object to make a forecast for May. Plot the forecasts. Note: use the prediction model you think is the most appropriate.

Step 1: Calculate hourly averages

```{r}

library(lubridate)

hourly_april <- april %>%
  mutate(hour = floor_date(datetime, unit = "hour")) %>%
  group_by(hour) %>%
  summarise(
    temperature = mean(Temperature_Comedor_Sensor, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(hourly_april)
```

Step 2: Create a time series

```{r}
temp_ts <- ts(
  hourly_april$temperature,
  frequency = 24
)

autoplot(temp_ts) +
  labs(
    title = "Hourly Average Temperature",
    x = "Time (days)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  )
```
Step 3: Fit a seasonal ETS model

```{r}

temp_model <- ets(temp_ts, model = "ANA")

summary(temp_model)
```
Forecasting May

```{r}

temp_forecast <- forecast(
  temp_model,
  h = 31 * 24
)

autoplot(temp_forecast) +
  labs(
    title = "Hourly Temperature Forecast for May",
    x = "Time (days)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  )


```

Step 1: Extract May observations

```{r}
nrow(may)
```

Step 2: Calculate hourly May temperatures

```{r}
hourly_may <- may %>%
  mutate(hour = floor_date(datetime, unit = "hour")) %>%
  group_by(hour) %>%
  summarise(
    temperature = mean(

head(hourly_may)
```

Step 3: Check whether May data is available

```{r}
nrow(hourly_may)
range(hourly_may$hour)
```

Compare forecasts with actual temperatures

Step 1: Extract the first 32 forecasts

```{r}
n <- nrow(hourly_may)

comparison <- data.frame(
  hour = hourly_may$hour,
  Actual = hourly_may$temperature,
  Forecast = as.numeric(temp_forecast$mean)[1:n]
)

head(comparison)
```

Step 2: Plot actual vs forecast

```{r}

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(comparison, aes(x = hour)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Actual, color = "Actual"),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Forecast, color = "Forecast"),
            linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs Forecast Temperature - May 2012",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Temperature (°C)",
    color = "Series"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

Step 3: Calculate out-of-sample errors

```{r}

RMSE <- sqrt(mean(
  (comparison$Actual - comparison$Forecast)^2
))

MAE <- mean(
  abs(comparison$Actual - comparison$Forecast)
)

MAPE <- mean(
  abs((comparison$Actual - comparison$Forecast) /
        comparison$Actual)
) * 100

data.frame(RMSE, MAE, MAPE)

```

2. Use one of the viewed methods (simple exponential smoothing, Holt, Holt-Winter) which is appropriated to your series. Justify your choice. Comment on your model’s parameter(s). How well does your model fit the data?

Create a clean time series
```{r}

swiss_clean <- switzerland %>%
  filter(Year >= 1980, !is.na(Exports))

swiss_ts <- ts(
  swiss_clean$Exports,

)

plot(
  swiss_ts,
```

Fit three forecasting models

```{r}
# Simple exponential smoothing
model_ses <- ses(swiss_ts, h = 5)

# Holt's linear trend

# Holt's damped trend
model_damped <- holt(
  swiss_ts,
  h = 5,
  damped = TRUE
)
```

Compare model accuracy

```{r}

comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("SES", "Holt", "Damped Holt"),

    accuracy(model_ses)[1, "RMSE"],

    accuracy(model_ses)[1, "MAE"],
    accuracy(model_holt)[1, "MAE"],
    accuracy(model_damped)[1, "MAE"]

)

comparison

```

**Exercise 5.**

Use the data set books from the package fpp3 to explore Holt’s exponential smoothing model with damping. Throughout this exercise, focus on how the state equations of the model can be used to simulate future paths and compute forecast-based quantities.

1. Convert the data to a tsibble object and fit a damped Holt model (ETS(A,Ad,N)) to the paperback series.

• Plot the observed series, fitted values, and 10-step-ahead forecasts.

• Report the estimated smoothing parameters and final state values.

```{r}
# Step 1: Convert books to a tsibble

books_ts <- tibble(
  Day = 1:nrow(books),
  Paperback = as.numeric(books[, "Paperback"]),
  Hardcover = as.numeric(books[, "Hardcover"])
) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = Day)

head(books_ts)
names(books_ts) # 'Day','Paperback','Hardcover'
is_tsibble(books_ts) # TRUE
```

```{r}
# Step 2: Fit ETS(A,Ad,N)

fit_damped <- books_ts %>%
  model(
    Damped = ETS(
      Paperback ~ error("A") +
        trend("Ad") +
        season("N")
    )
  )

report(fit_damped)


```

```{r}
# Step 3: Forecast 10 days ahead

fc_damped <- fit_damped %>%
  forecast(h = 10)

aug_damped <- augment(fit_damped)

books_ts %>%
  autoplot(Paperback, colour = "black") +
  autolayer(
    aug_damped,
    .fitted,
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  autolayer(
    fc_damped,
    colour = "blue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Damped Holt Model: Paperback Sales",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Number of Books Sold"
  )

```

```{r}

# Extract the final states
components(fit_damped)

# To inspect the final values:
components(fit_damped) |>
  tail(1)

```

2. Identify and write down the state equations corresponding to the damped Holt model based on the ETS table.

```{r}
# see written report
```

3. Using the state equations and the estimated parameters, simulate one future trajectory over the next h= 10 periods.

• Initialize the states with the final estimates.

• Generate Gaussian innovations εt∼N(0,^σ2).

• Plot the simulated path together with the historical series.

```{r}

set.seed(123)

# Estimated parameters
alpha <- 0.03259223
beta  <- 0.0001000242
phi   <- 0.98
sigma <- sqrt(1220.294)

# Final states
l <- 208.2084
b <- 0.9943547

# Forecast horizon
h <- 10

# Store simulated sales
sim_sales <- numeric(h)

for (i in 1:h) {

  # Generate a random innovation
  epsilon <- rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sigma)

  # Simulate next observation
  sim_sales[i] <- l + phi * b + epsilon

  # Update the states
  l_new <- l + phi * b + alpha * epsilon
  b_new <- phi * b + beta * epsilon

  l <- l_new
  b <- b_new
}

sim_sales

```

```{r}
# Plot the simulated trajectory

# Create a dataframe with simulated values
sim_df <- tibble(
  Day = 31:40,
  Simulated = sim_sales
)

# Plot historical and simulated sales
ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = books_ts,
    aes(x = Day, y = Paperback),
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = sim_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Simulated),
    colour = "blue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = sim_df,
    aes(x = Day, y = Simulated),
    colour = "blue"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 30.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "One Simulated Future Path: Paperback Sales",
    subtitle = "ETS(A,Ad,N) with Gaussian innovations",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Number of Books Sold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

4. Repeat the simulation Rtimes (e.g. R= 1000) and store all simulated paths. Use these to:

• Compute 95% prediction intervals for each horizon t+ 1,...,t+ h.

```{r}

# Step 1: Generate 1,000 simulated trajectories

set.seed(123)

R <- 1000
h <- 10

# Store simulations: rows = simulations, columns = days
sim_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = R, ncol = h)

for (r in 1:R) {

  # Reset states for each simulation
  l <- 208.2084
  b <- 0.9943547

  for (i in 1:h) {

    epsilon <- rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sigma)

    # Simulate sales
    sim_matrix[r, i] <- l + phi * b + epsilon

    # Update states
    l_new <- l + phi * b + alpha * epsilon
    b_new <- phi * b + beta * epsilon

    l <- l_new
    b <- b_new
  }
}

```

```{r}

# Step 2: Verify the simulations

dim(sim_matrix) # [1] 1000   10
# This means we have 1,000 simulated trajectories, each containing 10 future observations.

round(sim_matrix[1:5, ], 2)

```

```{r}

# Step 3: Calculate the 95% prediction intervals

# Calculate 95% prediction intervals
lower_95 <- apply(
  sim_matrix, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025
)

upper_95 <- apply(
  sim_matrix, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975
)

# Calculate mean simulated sales
mean_forecast <- colMeans(sim_matrix)

# Combine results
prediction_intervals <- tibble(
  Day = 31:40,
  Mean = mean_forecast,
  Lower_95 = lower_95,
  Upper_95 = upper_95
)

print(prediction_intervals)

```

```{r}

# Step 4: Plot the prediction intervals

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = books_ts,
    aes(x = Day, y = Paperback),
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = prediction_intervals,
    aes(
      x = Day,
      ymin = Lower_95,
      ymax = Upper_95
    ),
    fill = "skyblue",
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = prediction_intervals,
    aes(x = Day, y = Mean),
    colour = "blue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 30.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Monte Carlo 95% Prediction Intervals",
    x = "Day",
    y = "Paperback Sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

• Estimate the probability that sales increase for three consecutive days.

```{r}

# Step 7: Calculate the probability

# Function to check for 3 consecutive increases
three_increases <- function(x) {

  increases <- diff(x) > 0

  any(
    increases[-c(1, 2)] &
    increases[-c(1, length(increases))] &
    increases[-c(length(increases) - 1, length(increases))]
  )
}

# Apply to each simulated trajectory
results <- apply(sim_matrix, 1, three_increases)

# Estimated probability
probability <- mean(results)

probability

```
